_comment: Column-ordering conformance cases. Every runner reads this file, renders
each case in each listed format, RE-PARSES its own emitted bytes with an
order-preserving parser, and reports the observed column sequence.
The observation — not the rendered bytes — is what the orchestrator diffs.
Table padding and YAML block style differ legitimately across runtimes
(comfy-table pads, tabwriter does not; php emits '-' on its own line), so
raw bytes were never comparable. Column ORDER is what the contract pins,
and re-parsing the runtime's own output is how we observe it honestly.
spec    — ColumnSpec list, in list order. null means 'no ColumnSpec
supplied at all' (the payload-key fallback path).
rows    — payload rows. Key insertion order is significant and is
deliberately NOT the spec order in several cases.
cols    — the user's --cols override. [] means 'not supplied'.
formats — which formatters to exercise. 'portable' expands to the set
every runtime implements; 'extended' adds csv/text, which rs
header == key universally (contract rule 3), so a spec entry is one name.

cases.name: spec-order-vs-alphabetical
cases.why: ColumnSpec order is deliberately anti-alphabetical. A runtime that sorts its column map (rs's old BTreeMap) reorders to alpha,mid,zeta and is caught here.

cases.name: spec-order-vs-payload-order
cases.why: Payload keys are inserted alpha,mid,zeta while the ColumnSpec says zeta,alpha,mid. A runtime that infers columns from payload keys instead of honoring the spec is caught here (contract rule 1).

cases.name: cols-reorder-subset
cases.why: --cols selects a SUBSET in an order that matches neither the ColumnSpec list nor the payload keys. User order wins (contract rule 2): --cols reorders as well as selects. The requested order zeta,alpha is also anti-alphabetical, so a runtime that round-trips columns through an unordered map emits alpha,zeta and is caught rather than passing by coincidence.

cases.name: cols-reorder-against-declaration
cases.why: --cols asks for mid,zeta — a subset whose requested order is the REVERSE of the ColumnSpec/struct declaration order. Unlike cols-reorder-subset, the requested order here disagrees with declaration order, so a runtime that merely SELECTS without REORDERING emits zeta,mid and is caught. This is the case that separates 'honors --cols as a filter' from 'honors --cols as an ordering directive' (contract rule 2).

cases.name: no-spec-payload-fallback
cases.why: No ColumnSpec supplied at all. Payload key order is the fallback and ONLY then (contract rule 1). Keys are anti-alphabetical so a sorting runtime is caught.

cases.name: no-spec-cols-reorder
cases.why: No ColumnSpec, but --cols reorders. Contract rule 2 states the same precedence applies on the fallback path — no exception. Requested order is anti-alphabetical so an unordered-map round-trip is caught.

cases.name: empty-rows-with-spec
cases.why: Zero rows with a NON-EMPTY ColumnSpec. Emptiness is decided by ROW count, never header count, so no bare header row may be emitted (contract rule 4). A runtime guarding on header count instead emits 'zeta alpha mid' and is caught.

cases.name: cols-reorder-extended
cases.why: Same rule-2 assertion as cols-reorder-subset, on the csv/text formatters. rs and php do not ship these, so this case runs on py/ts/go only.

cases.name: spec-order-extended
cases.why: Rule-1 default ordering on the csv/text formatters. py/ts/go only.
